facts.text: In Old Regime France, society was divided into three estates: the First Estate was the clergy, the Second Estate was the nobility, and the Third Estate was everyone else, about 97 percent of the people, from peasants and city workers to the wealthy middle class, or bourgeoisie. The First Estate paid almost no taxes and the nobles were exempt from the main land tax, so the Third Estate paid most of the taxes to the crown. Costly wars, including the Seven Years' War and France's help for the American Revolution, left the crown deep in debt; it kept borrowing, the debt kept growing, and by 1788 the government was nearly bankrupt. A common mistake is to think the revolution happened because France was a poor country: France was one of Europe's richest and most populous kingdoms, but its government was broke because the privileged estates paid so little tax.

When King Louis XVI's finance ministers proposed taxing the nobles and clergy, the privileged refused in 1787 and insisted that only the Estates-General, a meeting of deputies from all three estates, could approve new taxes. Out of options, the king called the Estates-General to solve the debt, and it met at Versailles in May 1789 for the first time since 1614. Each estate voted as one bloc, called voting by order, so the First and Second Estates could outvote the Third two to one, even though the Third Estate had about as many deputies as the other two combined; the Third Estate demanded one vote per deputy and was refused. One way to picture it: France was a dinner table with a huge unpaid bill run up by the crown's wars; the clergy and noble diners refused to pay their share, the rule of one vote per diner let those two outvote the Third Estate, the diner who had always paid most of it, and so that diner got up and started a table of its own, the National Assembly.

Enlightenment ideas gave the Third Estate its argument: Rousseau taught that a government's power comes from the people, Montesquieu argued that power should be separated and limited, and the American Revolution had just shown that a people could replace a king's rule with a government based on rights. Led mostly by lawyers and other educated members of the bourgeoisie, the Third Estate's deputies declared themselves the National Assembly on June 17, 1789, claiming to speak for the whole nation; three days later, locked out of their meeting hall, they met on an indoor tennis court and swore the Tennis Court Oath, promising not to separate until France had a constitution. Meanwhile a bad harvest in 1788 sent bread prices soaring, and by 1789 bread could take more than half of a working family's income, so hunger and anger spread among ordinary people in Paris. When the king gathered troops near Paris and dismissed a popular minister, Parisian crowds backed the National Assembly, and on July 14, 1789 they stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, to seize gunpowder; it held only seven prisoners, but its fall showed that the king had lost control of his capital.

The result was power shifting from the king to an assembly that claimed to represent the people: in August 1789 the National Assembly abolished the privileges of the nobles and clergy and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which said that people are born free and equal in rights, and later the revolution turned more radical. The same pattern appears earlier in the course, in England: Charles I ruled without Parliament for eleven years, but in 1640 he needed money to fight a rebellion in Scotland, so he had to call Parliament; Parliament used its control over taxes to demand limits on his power, the quarrel became the English Civil War in 1642, Parliament's army defeated the royal side, and Charles I was tried and beheaded in 1649.

lesson_markdown:
## Why did the French Revolution happen?

**How does a government run out of money and end up handing power to an assembly?**

In 1789, France's crown was nearly bankrupt, and the people who could pay refused. The core idea: the crown went broke, the privileged refused to pay, so calling the Estates-General let the Third Estate seize power. This lesson simplifies the story to its main causes.

### Picture a dinner bill

Imagine a dinner table with a huge unpaid bill, run up by the crown's wars. The clergy and noble diners refuse to pay their share. The rule is one vote per diner, so those two outvote the Third Estate, the diner who has always paid most of it. So that diner gets up and starts a table of its own: the National Assembly.

### Who paid in Old Regime France?

| Estate | Who | Taxes |
|---|---|---|
| First Estate | The clergy | Almost none |
| Second Estate | The nobles | Exempt from the main land tax |
| Third Estate | Everyone else, about 97% of people | Most of the taxes |

### The chain of causes

1. **The crown went deep into debt.** Costly wars, including the Seven Years' War and France's help for the American Revolution, left it nearly bankrupt by 1788.
2. **The privileged blocked reform.** When the king's ministers proposed taxing nobles and clergy, the privileged refused in 1787 and said only the Estates-General could approve new taxes.
3. **The king had to call the Estates-General.** This meeting of deputies from all three estates opened at Versailles in May 1789, for the first time since 1614.
4. **The voting favoured the privileged.** Each estate voted as one bloc, so the First and Second Estates could outvote the Third two to one, even though the Third had about as many deputies as the other two combined.

The Third Estate demanded one vote per deputy and was refused. What do you think its deputies did next? On June 17, 1789, they declared themselves the National Assembly, claiming to speak for the whole nation.

Enlightenment ideas gave them their argument: Rousseau taught that a government's power comes from the people. Their leaders were mostly lawyers and other educated members of the bourgeoisie. Three days later, locked out of their hall, they met on an indoor tennis court and swore the **Tennis Court Oath**, promising not to separate until France had a constitution.

### Bread and the Bastille

A bad harvest in 1788 sent bread prices soaring, and by 1789 bread could take more than half of a working family's income. When the king gathered troops near Paris, angry crowds backed the National Assembly. On July 14, 1789, they stormed the **Bastille**, a royal fortress and prison, to seize gunpowder. It held only seven prisoners, but its fall showed that the king had lost control of his capital.

### A common mistake

A common mistake is to think the revolution happened because France was a poor country. In fact, France was one of Europe's richest kingdoms; its government was broke because the privileged estates paid so little tax.

### You've seen this before

The same pattern appears in England. Charles I ruled without Parliament for eleven years, but in 1640 he needed money to fight a rebellion in Scotland, so he had to call Parliament. Parliament used its control over taxes to demand limits on his power, and the quarrel became the English Civil War in 1642. Parliament's army defeated the royal side, and Charles I was tried and beheaded in 1649.

### What comes next

In August 1789, the National Assembly abolished the privileges of the nobles and clergy and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which said people are born free and equal in rights. Later, the revolution turned more radical.

### Check yourself

If the First and Second Estates had agreed to pay new taxes in 1787, why might the Estates-General never have been called at all?

Curious about any step? Ask a follow-up question.
